sources: Lahore: A Framework for Urban Conservation (Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme, 2019)

landmarks.name: Sheesh Mahal
landmarks.description: One of the most celebrated monuments in Lahore Fort, the Sheesh Mahal (Palace of Mirrors) was built by Shah Jahan as part of the Shah Burj complex. Its facade consists of five multi-cusped marble arches supported by coupled columns. The interior walls and ceilings are encrusted with intricate mirror and coloured-glass mosaic work (kund-kari), reflecting candlelight to create a dazzling effect. The structure is rated as having 'outstanding significance' in the 2018 UNESCO Master Plan for Lahore Fort.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — UNESCO World Heritage Site component
image_keywords: Sheesh Mahal Lahore Fort interior mirrors
landmarks.photo_tips: Best shot is the marble facade from the courtyard. Interior mirror-work needs supplemental light. Shoot early morning to avoid crowds.

landmarks.name: Alamgiri Gate
landmarks.description: The main western entrance gate to Lahore Fort, built by Emperor Aurangzeb (also known as Alamgir) in 1673. The gate faces the Badshahi Mosque across the Hazuri Bagh. It is a monumental structure flanked by two large semi-circular bastions decorated with white marble and faience tile-work. The gate served as the ceremonial royal entrance during the Mughal period.
landmarks.significance: High — primary Fort entrance, faces Badshahi Mosque
landmarks.status: Open to visitors — main entry point
landmarks.photo_tips: Wide-angle shot from Hazuri Bagh captures gate and Badshahi Mosque together. Golden hour (5–6 PM in summer) is ideal.

landmarks.name: Picture Wall
landmarks.description: The Picture Wall is a 1,450-foot-long exterior wall running along the northern and western faces of Lahore Fort. Built during the reign of Emperor Jahangir, it is decorated with elaborate glazed-tile mosaic work (kashi-kari) depicting hunting scenes, combat between mythological animals, polo matches, portraits of courtiers, and geometric patterns. It is considered one of the largest examples of Mughal decorative tile-work in existence. Conservation of this wall is a major ongoing project by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — largest Mughal tile-work panel in existence
image_keywords: Picture Wall Lahore Fort tile mosaic
landmarks.photo_tips: Walk along the outer perimeter for full panoramic shots. Closeups reveal individual tile scenes. Overcast days give better colour saturation than direct sun.

landmarks.name: Diwan-e-Aam
landmarks.description: The Diwan-e-Aam (Hall of Public Audience) is where the Mughal emperors held public court sessions to hear petitions from ordinary citizens. The structure is a colonnaded hall facing an open quadrangle. It was used by Shah Jahan and successive emperors to dispense justice and receive public delegations. The building's architecture features multi-cusped arches and a raised platform where the emperor's throne was placed.
image_keywords: Diwan-e-Aam Lahore Fort hall public audience
landmarks.photo_tips: Shoot from inside the quadrangle looking towards the hall for best architectural framing. Morning light from the east illuminates the facade well.

landmarks.name: Jahangir's Quadrangle
landmarks.description: The largest quadrangle within Lahore Fort, built during the reign of Emperor Jahangir. The courtyard was recently restored with its historical water features and pools reinstated based on examples from the Shalimar Garden. The four sides of the quadrangle are lined with elegant arcaded halls. The northern facade, known as the Daulat Khana-e-Khaas-o-Aam, is a masterpiece of early Mughal architecture. The quadrangle served as the imperial residential and administrative core of the Fort.
landmarks.photo_tips: The restored water pools create beautiful reflections. Shoot from the corners diagonally to capture full arcade depth. Best in soft morning light.

landmarks.name: Naulakha Pavilion
landmarks.description: The Naulakha Pavilion (named for its reputed construction cost of nine lakhs of rupees) is a small but exquisitely crafted white marble pavilion built by Shah Jahan. It features a distinctive curved Bengal-style (bangaldar) roof, a uniquely elegant form rarely seen in Lahore Fort's predominantly flat-roofed Mughal architecture. The interior and exterior surfaces are decorated with pietra dura inlay (parchinkari) — coloured stone inlaid in intricate floral and geometric patterns.
landmarks.significance: High — unique bangaldar roof; finest pietra dura work in the Fort
image_keywords: Shah Jahan bangaldar roof pietra dura
landmarks.photo_tips: Close-up shots of the pietra dura inlay are stunning. The curved roof is best photographed from a slight distance and low angle.

landmarks.name: Moti Masjid
landmarks.description: The Moti Masjid (Pearl Mosque) is a small but elegant private mosque built within Lahore Fort for the imperial family's personal prayers. Constructed of white marble, it features three domed bays and a rectangular prayer chamber. The mosque is notable for its fine proportions and purity of white marble. A similar mosque of the same name exists in Delhi's Red Fort and Agra Fort, reflecting Shah Jahan's characteristic architectural language.
landmarks.significance: Medium-High — example of imperial private mosque architecture
image_keywords: Moti Masjid Lahore Fort pearl mosque marble domes
landmarks.photo_tips: The three domes are best seen from the courtyard. Shoot against blue sky for contrast with white marble. Interior has soft diffused light.

landmarks.name: Hazuri Bagh
landmarks.quadrangle: External — between Fort and Badshahi Mosque
landmarks.description: Hazuri Bagh is the formal garden located between Lahore Fort's Alamgiri Gate and the Badshahi Mosque. Built by Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1818, the garden contains his marble baradari (pavilion) at its centre, which served as his royal audience hall in the open air. The baradari is a finely crafted twelve-door marble pavilion set on a raised platform. The garden layout follows the traditional Mughal charbagh (four-garden) design. It offers one of the finest views of both the Fort and the Mosque simultaneously.
landmarks.significance: High — rare Sikh-period monument; connects Fort and Badshahi Mosque visually
image_keywords: Hazuri Bagh Lahore baradari Ranjit Singh
landmarks.photo_tips: This is the best spot to capture all three — Alamgiri Gate, the Baradari, and Badshahi Mosque in one frame. Visit at golden hour for stunning light.

landmarks.name: Shah Burj
landmarks.description: Shah Burj (Royal Tower) is the north-western complex of Lahore Fort, encompassing the Sheesh Mahal, Naulakha Pavilion, and the Summer Palace. It is one of the most ornate sections of the Fort, built primarily by Shah Jahan and later embellished by Jahangir. The complex includes an octagonal bastion at the north corner decorated with the Picture Wall below. The Shah Burj complex was the private royal quarters and is considered the jewel of Lahore Fort.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — contains the Sheesh Mahal, Naulakha, and Picture Wall
image_keywords: Shah Burj Lahore Fort Sheesh Mahal complex
landmarks.photo_tips: The octagonal bastion at the north corner gives an elevated view over the entire complex and the city beyond.

landmarks.name: Akbari Gate
landmarks.description: The Akbari Gate is the oldest surviving gate of Lahore Fort, built during the reign of Emperor Akbar as part of his early fortification programme. It connects the Diwan-e-Aam quadrangle to the eastern sector of the Fort. The gate reflects Akbar's early architectural style, which blends Timurid Central Asian forms with Indian craftsmanship. It was one of several gates constructed to compartmentalise the Fort's functions.
landmarks.significance: Medium-High — oldest surviving gate in the Fort
image_keywords: Akbari Gate Lahore Fort Akbar oldest gate
landmarks.photo_tips: Best captured in context with the Diwan-e-Aam quadrangle behind. Look for the worn stone carvings on the doorframe.

landmarks.name: Imperial Kitchens
landmarks.description: The Imperial Kitchens are a large complex of vaulted service buildings in the south-western part of Lahore Fort that once served the royal household. The kitchens are notable for their massive chimneys, ventilation shafts, and storage chambers designed to support large-scale food preparation for the imperial court. They are currently being adapted for reuse as a museum and visitor facility as part of the AKTC/WCLA conservation programme, documented in the 2018 Master Plan.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving service complex; being adaptively reused
image_keywords: Imperial Kitchens Lahore Fort vaulted chambers
landmarks.photo_tips: The vaulted brick ceilings are architecturally striking. Chimneys make for dramatic vertical framing shots.
